data.title: A virtual tour through the glitz and glam of Fierce Pharma Week
data.description:
With many of the healthcare industry’s top marketing minds converging in the City of Brotherly Love this past week, the galvanizing power of humor, authenticity and a little outside-the-box thinking in an ever-changing consumer landscape was again at the forefront of Fierce Pharma Week.

Running Monday through Thursday at the Pennsylvania Convention Center in Philadelphia, the second incarnation of Fierce Pharma Week covered a wide range of topics spanning marketing, medical affairs, public relations and communications, and commercialization. A highlight of the festivities was the 2026 Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards, replete with trophies, prosecco and a standing ovation for CineHealth Lifetime Achievement Award winner and Emmy-winning journalist Maria Menounos.

But in between the action, there was plenty more fun to be had and just as many nuggets of wisdom (and pretzels) on offer across a swath of booths, exhibits, panels and one-on-one interviews populating the convention center’s stages and exhibit hall.

Between a Cadent-sponsored claw machine, a Health Monitor aura portrait studio, a Syneos Health magician, a Sermo AI fortune teller and more, the lively exhibit floor was abuzz with energy and flowing with unique networking opportunities. Attendees’ hunger for sweet treats and fresh marketing insights was satiated all week long, whether through the packed schedule of sessions and speakers or the custom pancake artist and roaming cannoli offerings (please don’t ask our reporters how many cannoli they consumed).
Fierce Pharma Week 2026

Plus, the puppy pen from last year’s inaugural event made its triumphant return, ensuring all attendees could access some fuzzy, four-legged comfort on demand. Some may even be bringing a new fluffy friend home with them. Each of the puppies seen wagging around the GoodRx Puppy Park garnered adoption applications, Fierce can confirm.

How pharmas connect with patients and the broader communities they serve can be more art than science, but one theme that rang true across panels and events was the importance of sincerity.

Comedian Damon Wayans, a patient advocate and spokesperson for the humor-forward Genentech campaign “All Eyes of DME,” said that element is at the heart of his work with the Roche subsidiary to raise awareness of diabetes-related vision concerns.

In outlining his health advocacy journey in an interview with Fierce this week, Wayans recalled the type 2 diabetes diagnosis he received in his late 40s, connecting it to his own mother’s experience with the disease.

After taking steps to manage his condition, Wayans now carries himself as an example to his community and close circle. In terms of the Genentech campaign, he said a more relatable approach to DME awareness is one he had a personal hand in, recognizing that humor is a “great way to reach people’s hearts.”

Humor also helped carry home a Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards win for Novartis and Digitas’ “Relax Your Tight End” campaign at this year’s event, featuring NFL star tight ends like Rob Gronkowski and Tony Gonzalez encouraging prostate cancer screenings with the assurance, “relax, it’s just a blood test.”
Fierce Pharma Week 2026

Argenx took a similar approach and scored its second Marketing Awards win with its “CIDP Unscripted” online learning video series, which partners with legendary improv troupe the Upright Citizens Brigade to help patients with chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) build confidence and improve communication with doctors and their families.

Those genuine connections, whether formed through humor or vulnerability, continued to carry weight during the awards gala when Menounos appeared to a standing ovation as she was honored by CineHealth for her courage in sharing her story of battling two types of cancer and other health issues.

Tracey Yaw, festival director of the CineHealth International Health and Wellness Film and Video Festival, which was again incorporated into the Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards this year, told Fierce in an interview that she’s “so passionate about this and being able to bring people’s stories to life and giving them a platform.”

Even beyond the vast glass windows of the Pennsylvania Convention Center, conversations were focused on how companies connect with consumers, who those consumers are and what they want as the industry responds to a rapidly evolving commercial reality.
Fierce Pharma Week 2026

The sentiment was on display in a Fierce interview with Novo CEO Mike Doustdar earlier this week, with the helmsman sitting down virtually to discuss a key rebrand that has seen the Danish drugmaker drop the Nordisk from its name in most of its everyday branding.

With that change also came a modification to Novo’s purpose and a declaration of “The Novo Way,” which includes customer obsession, competitiveness, clarity and, finally, care and integrity.

Meanwhile, in shifting to a mantra that “Lasting Health Starts Now,” Novo has moved away from its previous declaration of purpose to drive change to defeat serious chronic diseases.

“Increasingly, the people we serve tell you that we cannot see ourselves in that statement,” Doustdar explained during the conversation with Fierce.
Fierce Pharma Week 2026

Many of Novo’s customers don’t consider themselves patients or people with a chronic disease, especially those taking a medication for weight loss, Doustdar pointed out.

“That disconnect makes you go back and think: How can I realign myself again to those I’m serving,” he added.

As for the ever-important question of conference swag, we’d be remiss not to mention that Fierce Pharma Marketing’s Zoey Becker amassed a veritable menagerie of stuffed critters, including a zebra, panther and meerkat. Regarding her cat’s reaction to these new friends, Fierce will keep you posted.

data.title: FDA approves Ultragenyx gene therapy after prior rejection
data.description:
Ultragenyx scored a belated regulatory win with the FDA approval of a first-in-disease gene therapy, giving the company a boost after a previous regulatory rejection and a recent late-stage setback.

The FDA has approved Ultragenyx’s Fayuvi as the first treatment for children with mucopolysaccharidosis type IIIA (MPS IIIA), also known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A, a rare genetic disorder. 

MPS III is a neurodegenerative disorder, with MPS IIIA the most common form. Due to a change in the SGSH gene, patients with MPS IIIA cannot make enough of an enzyme called sulfamidase. Without the enzyme, complex sugar molecules called heparan sulfate build up in cells and damage the brain, causing children to lose cognitive, language and other developmental abilities over time.

According to Ultragenyx, an estimated 3,000 to 5,000 patients in the developed world are affected by Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Fayuvi, previously known as UX111, uses an adeno-associated viral vector to deliver a working copy of the SGSH gene into the patient’s cells. It marks the first FDA-approved therapy designed to address the underlying disease; previously, treatment for MPS IIIA focused on managing symptoms. 

“The approval of Fayuvi marks a historic moment for children and families living with MPS IIIA, which is a disease that has, until now, offered no approved treatment to alter its devastating course,” Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas said in a Sept. 17 statement. “Gene therapy holds tremendous promise for rare diseases like Sanfilippo syndrome type A, and this milestone reflects the FDA's commitment to action.”  

The road to this milestone was not without hurdles for Ultragenyx. Last year, the FDA declined to approve the one-time gene therapy due to manufacturing-related issues at Ultragenyx’s own gene therapy production facility and a third-party manufacturer. The California biotech has publicly stated that it’s producing Fayuvi at its facility in Bedford, Massachusetts, and through Andelyn Biosciences in Columbus, Ohio. 

The FDA accepted the company’s resubmission in April and put it under priority review.

The FDA evaluated data from a small group of patients from a single-arm trial, which measured levels of heparan sulfate in cerebrospinal fluid as a biomarker, as well as neurodevelopmental outcomes and compared them with natural history. 

Among 17 children under 2 years of age or with earlier-stage of the disease at the time of treatment, a one-time intravenous infusion of Fayuvi led to a positive 23.2-point treatment effect in cognitive score as measured by Bayley-III compared to natural history data. 

Eight children reached a 36-month cognitive development age, whereas no one in the natural history cohort reached this milestone.

Among 10 older or later-stage children, retention of functional abilities was observed in at least one of three areas at the time of their last assessment, exceeding typical decline patterns in untreated children with Sanfilippo syndrome Type A.

The above data were presented in February and submitted to the FDA as part of Ultragenyx’s application for Fayuvi.

“We recognize the profound urgency of making this therapy available to families, and our focus now is on supporting timely access in the U.S. as we work closely with treatment centers and payers to support families on the gene therapy treatment journey,” Ultragenyx CEO Emil Kakkis, M.D., Ph.D., said in a Sept. 17 statement. 

Fayuvi marks Ultragenyx’s second FDA approval in less than a month, following an FDA accelerated approval for its other AAV gene therapy, Genglycos, for the rare genetic disorder glycogen storage disease type Ia (GSDIa). 

However, the company is still reeling from a major clinical setback earlier this month, which saw its Angelman syndrome candidate, an antisense oligonucleotide therapy called apazunersen, crash out in phase 3 development. Following the phase 3 Aspire trial flop, Ultragenyx’s stock price hit its all-time low this month, as the company mulls potential “significant expense reductions.”

Fayuvi’s approval also comes in the wake of a turbulent time, during which the FDA’s former leadership took a stringent approach to rare disease approvals. The heightened regulatory scrutiny led to a demonstration co-staged by National MPS Society at the FDA’s White Oak campus in March. Since then, the FDA has approved Denali Therapeutics’ enzyme replacement therapy Avlayah for Hunter syndrome, or MPS II. 

The agency also walked back a previous request for Regenxbio to incorporate a control arm for its MPS II gene therapy candidate RGX-121, although the Maryland biotech’s FDA refiling plan was recently stalled because of a clinical hold following a safety signal in a sister program designed for MPS I.

data.title: Sun Pharma shines a light on alopecia areata in new campaign
data.description:
Sun Pharma is teaming up with fashion designer Christian Siriano for a new educational campaign focused on the positives of regrowing lost hair.

The Indian company last July launched Leqselvi (deuruxolitinib) in the U.S., an oral med designed for adults with severe alopecia areata.

Alopecia areata is an autoimmune condition in which the immune system mistakenly attacks hair follicles, causing hair loss. Hair can fall out in small, round patches, most commonly on the scalp, though some patients can lose all the hair on their scalp or body. The condition may affect up to 2.5% of the U.S. population during their lifetime.

“Regrowth Restyled” looks to “celebrate how beauty, confidence, and self-expression” can be a part of the hair regrowth journey, Sun said in a statement. The company is seeking to remove stigma while also boosting awareness of its med.

Related

Sun Pharma's alopecia med Leqselvi hits US market after Incyte patent settlement

The campaign dovetails with Alopecia Areata Awareness Month in September and sees Sun working with Siriano to create a one-of-a-kind wearable garment “inspired by the journey of hair regrowth.”

The piece debuted following New York Fashion Week on Sept. 17.

“As a designer, I've always believed style is a form of self-expression, and for adults living with severe alopecia areata, hair loss can complicate that expression in ways that go far beyond appearance,” said Siriano in a release.

“I'm excited to participate in this campaign because it creates a platform to broaden the conversation around alopecia areata and reminds anyone navigating this condition that self-expression is uniquely theirs and does not have to wait.”

Sun hasn’t broken down sales of the drug, but after its U.S. launch last year, Shrikant Akolkar, an analyst at Nuvama Institutional Equities, said Leqselvi could generate up to $400 million in sales by 2030, with peak sales potential of $900 million.

The drug competes with Pfizer’s rival Litfulo and Lilly’s Olumiant, which was developed in collaboration with Incyte and hit blockbuster status last year.

data.title: Comedian Damon Wayans on humor, relatability and DME awareness
data.description:
Acclaimed comedian, actor and writer Damon Wayans recently added patient advocate and spokesperson to his resume through a humor-forward Genentech campaign, “All Eyes on DME,” that raises awareness of diabetes-related vision concerns.  

“It’s a good feeling,” the Emmy-nominated “In Living Color” star told Fierce in an interview following his keynote panel at Fierce Pharma Week. 

“Being a comedian is great when you’re on stage,” Wayans said. But being an advocate for change, he said, is something that can be done “all day, every day.” 

The comedian’s health advocacy journey traces its roots to his type 2 diabetes diagnosis in his late 40s. By then, Wayans was all too familiar with the disease after watching his mother suffer from it. Growing up, “we didn’t really know what it was,” he said. 

Instead of dealing with diabetes like his mother, who he said “never really got control over what she had,” Wayans took a different path to disease management, gaining a better understand of his body’s reactions through a glucose monitor which was, to him, “the greatest thing ever.” 

Now, he stands as an example to his community and close circle, proving that “there’s a different way” to enjoy a quality, although “very disciplined” life while managing diabetes. 

Related

Standout pharma marketing takes the stage at the 2026 Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards

In “All Eyes on DME,” Genentech partnered with advocacy group diaTribe to shine a light on and destigmatize diabetes eye complication diabetic macular edema (DME) through a multi-channel U.S. campaign starring Wayans, a paid Genentech spokesperson. A series of videos from an event that ran with the campaign features the “Saturday Night Live” alum talking DME in a familiar setting for him: on stage, mic in hand during a stand-up comedy routine. In his monologue, Wayans weaves comedy and relatable aging experiences with the real health issue of “funny vision.” 

Wayans continues to share his journey with diabetes throughout the set and further touches on DME through a story about a man he met in the eye doctor’s waiting room. Ultimately, Wayans emphasizes that “early action matters” and those with diabetes should ask their own doctors about DME.

The relatable approach to DME awareness is one he intentionally crafted as a “great way to reach people’s hearts,” he explained. 

It’s a thread that’s carried throughout his career in stand-up and film. When his two sons were young, Wayans took them to see the “Ninja Turtles” movie, unintentionally witnessing firsthand how relatability can reach audiences in a different way.  

“As soon as the movie started, my son goes, ‘that's me,’” the actor recounted. “He picked who he was, and then my other son goes. ‘I'm Donatello.’ And what that taught me right there in that moment is that people do that when they go to the movies. They go to the movie and they see themselves in these characters, and that's how they go on this journey.” 

The anecdote applies to disease education as well, as audiences can walk away “seeing you in me without being judged,” he explained. “I think people like the sincerity of it.”

The humor Wayans brought to the campaign was meant to break down barriers of stigmas and fear, a prevailing issue in DME treatment that Genentech didn’t entirely expect. 

“We thought it was an awareness problem,” Genentech chief marketing officer Zoë Harris Lazarre, Ph.D., explained in a separate interview. 

As it turns out, the low levels of eye screenings seen in diabetes patients wasn’t as simple as awareness on its own. Around 60% of Americans living with diabetes miss their recommended eye exams, Genentech found. With the U.S. diabetes patient population projected to reach 55 million by 2030 and people of color being two to three times more likely to experience sight-threatening diabetes-related conditions such as DME, vision loss within at-risk communities marks a significant “escalating public health issue,” according to the company. 

Upon working with diaTribe and talking with patients, especially in groups disproportionately affected by DME, the real “emotional barrier” unfolded, Lazarre said. 

“What’s the antidote to fear? It’s humor,” Lazarre explained. “Humor creates connection. It opens a difficult conversation, and it really allows you to talk about those things that are scary.”

Wayan’s work with Genentech on “All Eyes on DME” included a panel event, in which one panelist shared her experience with DME. Her sight visions inspired Wayans’ to get his eyes checked promptly upon returning from the event, he shared. Although his sight issues were glasses prescription-based, seeing advanced ocular technology first-hand was an “empowering” experience, he said. 

“Fear is in the unknown, and feeling like you’re just hopeless,” he explained. To mitigate the fear of the unknown, Wayans emphasizes the importance of staying on top of potential health problems by seeking out research and treatments. 

“I’d rather go out knowing that I fought as hard as I could, even if I do lose my eyes or lose the battle with diabetes, at least I know I did everything I can,” Wayans said. “And my children, my grandchildren, my brothers and sisters know that I put up a fight, and that's really what it's about. But knowledge is power. You can't fight what you can't see or don't know.”

data.title: Lilly boxes up fresh produce to cultivate Alzheimer’s awareness
data.description:
Eli Lilly is marking World Alzheimer’s Day with a partnership to distribute 13,500 boxes of brain-healthy fresh produce and educational materials to underserved senior populations across the U.S.

Lilly, which sells the Alzheimer’s disease medicine Kisunla, has partnered with Planet Harvest and Thrive Global on the initiative. Together, the partners are shipping boxes containing 12 to 15 pounds of fruits and vegetables, chosen for their links to healthy aging and cognitive wellness, and a pouch of salmon to people. Recipients will also get recipes suggesting ways to quickly and easily turn the produce into meals. 

The boxes will go to “underserved senior populations and communities in 10 U.S. markets where food insecurity and social isolation remain a significant challenge,” Jennifer Oleksiw, global chief customer officer at Lilly, told Fierce. 

Each box contains a QR code linking to Lilly’s Brain Health Matters website, which features information about the stages, signs and symptoms of Alzheimer’s. Lilly will assess the impact of the initiative by confirming that the boxes reach their intended recipients and by looking at how many people scan the QR code to visit its website.

“We will be monitoring, ‘What type of information are they engaging with? What do they need to see more of? What did they need to see less of?’” Oleksiw said. Lilly will use the data to inform its actions to expand the online services that it provides to meet patients’ needs. 

The use of produce boxes as a vehicle for brain health education reflects evidence that lifestyle changes could delay or prevent many cases of dementia, including Alzheimer’s. A 2024 study found that about 45% of dementia cases could be prevented by managing 14 risk factors, including hypertension, obesity, high LDL cholesterol and diabetes.

Lilly leveraged existing partnerships to deliver the produce and brain-health messaging. The drugmaker previously partnered with Thrive to add behavior change tools and resources to its direct-to-consumer platform, LillyDirect. Over the past year, Lilly and Thrive have worked with food supply chain company Planet Harvest to deliver boxes in states including Arkansas and Florida. 

The partners helped Lilly to identify locations with the biggest need for its brain-health boxes. With the initiative underway, Lilly is now looking to expand the scheme to reach more people across the U.S.

“The goal is that we would do this consistently,” Oleksiw said. “This will not be a one-and-done opportunity, but instead something that we expect to expand on and scale as we move forward.”

data.title: Novartis, GSK and more shine at Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards
data.description:
Major drugmakers and top agencies alike earned their flowers at the annual Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards gala in Philadelphia, which passed out winning trophies across a total of 20 unique categories. 

Each year, the awards are doled out to pharma marketers whose creativity, strategy, impact and innovation hit the mark, with categories spanning the marketing, advertising and PR gambit. During Fierce Pharma Week on Sept. 15, marketers flocked to the National Constitution Center in Philadelphia for a glitzy night of celebrations for their hard-earned honors, complete with a red carpet and a prosecco-centered cocktail hour. 

Out of the 20 awards presented this year, two new categories hit the stage in Point of Care Marketing and Data-Driven Campaign. The award for Data-Driven Campaign, which was sponsored by Doceree, went to Tarsus Pharmaceuticals and Moon Rabbit for “Xdemvy: Finding the Invisible Patient,” a growth-driving Xdemvy project that used a predictive framework to identify patients who hadn’t yet been diagnosed with demodex blepharitis. 

Also sponsored by Doceree, the Point of Care Marketing award was given to “Fintepla Video Book” by UCB, OLIXIR New York and Spectrum Science. The interactive video book is aimed at caregivers of children with rare diseases Dravet syndrome and Lennox-Gastaut syndrome who may feel overwhelmed and offers a educative physical and digital resource, guided by an on-screen guide named Faye who introduces UCB’s Fintepla. 

Elsewhere across the winner’s line-up, some of the unique and innovative swings pharma marketers took this year were rewarded in turn. GSK and Chandler Chicco Agency, for one, took home the Pharma TV gold for their sponsored Lifetime original movie, “Pretty Hurts.” The movie was the first pharma-sponsored flick to air on Lifetime and marked an extension of GSK’s Ask2BSure meningitis awareness campaign, featuring a meningitis-centered storyline and a cast of familiar faces such as Haylie Duff. 

Related

Sanofi, Gilead, Acadia win big at the 2025 Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards

GSK also went home with the Innovation Challenge win for “The Odds,” an Endelmen Canada-partnered campaign that took a behavioral science approach to education for GSK’s shingles vaccine Shingrix. The spot ran across connected TV, digital, out-of-home, social and retail channels and sought to address the optimism bias often encountered in preventative healthcare by reminding viewers of the jarring 1 in 3 odds of getting shingles, a striking stat compared to the 1 in 334 chances of a skiing injury, as one example points out. 

Other big winners, meanwhile, represented shining examples of a familiar, influencer-driven style, such as Novartis and Digitas’ star-studded “Relax Your Tight End” ad. First aired at the Super Bowl LX this Feb., the humorous spot featured a roster of NFL star tight ends including Rob Gronkowski and Tony Gonzalez to promote prostate cancer screenings and remind viewers to “relax, it’s just a blood test.” 

“We want to make sure it’s memorable—that they’re going to go and do something with it after they see it,” Novartis U.S. president Victor Bulto told Fierce earlier this year. 

For the ad, as well as the associated social media push, “Relax Your Tight End” won Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards for Influencer-Driven Campaign and Social Media for Consumer. 

Another repeat winner was argenx, which swept in both the Website for Consumer and Online Video and Film categories for its “CIDP Unscripted” with Avalere Health. "CIDP Unscripted" is an online learning video series that highlights the unpredictability of chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) by partnering with renowned improv troupe the Upright Citizens Brigade. The fun yet educational videos present improv tools that patients can harness to build confidence and develop better communications with their doctors and families.

This year’s Fierce Pharma Marketing Awards night again incorporated CineHealth and its 4th Annual International Health and Wellness Film Festival Awards, which gave out its own set of awards including the Lifetime Achievement Award. 

"I am so passionate about this and being able to bring people's stories to life and giving them a platform," Tracey Yaw, festival director of the CineHealth International Health and Wellness Film and Video Festival said in an interview with Fierce. 

CineHealth's Lifetime Achievement Award went to television host and health advocate Maria Menounos, who was honored on stage for her bravery in sharing her empowering story of battling two types of cancer and other health issues. Menounos' appearance resulted in a standing ovation from the crowd, which was followed by a teary-eyed speech from the Emmy-award winning journalist. 

Then it was time for the agency of the year and the marketer of the year. New York-based independent agency Moon Rabbit hopped onto stage as the top agency of the year, winning over finalists such as the Deerfield Group and /prompt. 

Meanwhile, the honor of marketer of the year went to Supernus Pharmaceuticals’ VP of marketing Rebecca Lannan. Lannan was nominated by Burson and was one of three finalists from the pharma side, with others including Ionis’ Tricia reeves and Tarsus’ Jason Alongi. 

Read on for the full list of 2026 Fierce Pharma Marketing Award winners. 

 

Best Use of AI: 

“Live for What You Love” from Bayer and PulsePoint

data.title: Ex-PHM CEO Andrea Palmer takes top job at Assembled Intelligence
data.description:
Former Publicis Health Media (PHM) CEO Andrea Palmer has revealed her next post. The executive has taken the CEO position at Assembled Intelligence, the agency that Minds + Assembly launched last year to integrate its flurry of acquisitions.

Palmer climbed the ladder at PHM, becoming president in 2019 and taking over as CEO in 2024. News of Palmer’s departure emerged last month, when PHM appointed Stephen Farquhar as CEO. At the time, it was unclear why Palmer, who spent more than 15 years at Publicis, had stepped down as CEO or where she would land next. 

Assembled Intelligence filled in some of the gaps this week. Effective immediately, Palmer has replaced Mark Lydiatt as CEO. Lydiatt will continue to support the company as a member of the board and as a strategic advisor to the leadership team.

Assembled Intelligence cited Palmer’s experience integrating AI and programmatic marketing into PHM’s infrastructure in its overview of her background. Palmer outlined how she plans to use her experience to lead the team at a time when AI and consumer expectations are changing quickly. 

“My focus is on bringing together science, creative, media, data analytics and market access capabilities in ways this industry hasn't seen before, and to help our clients move first and move boldly,” Palmer said. 

Assembled Intelligence named Chuck Hemann as chief business and AI officer in June. Lydiatt, then the CEO of Assembled Intelligence, framed the appointment in the context of the rise of AI platforms that are “opening entirely new service models that weren’t economically or practically feasible before.”

Lydiatt co-founded Boldscience in 2020. The medical communications agency joined forces with Minds + Assembly in 2024. Lydiatt became CEO of Minds + Assembly as part of the deal. The Boldscience pact was part of a string of deals that Minds + Assembly struck after receiving investment from Amulet Capital Partners. In quick succession, the agency bought Awaken Interactive, HashtagHealth and Stratevi.

Last year, Minds + Assembly launched Assembled Intelligence to unite the capabilities acquired across its deal spree. As Assembled Intelligence’s second CEO, Palmer will work closely with Amulet Capital as she oversees the next stage of the agency’s plan.

data.title: Novo CEO talks embracing change and staying bullish amid rebrand
data.description:
Novo CEO Mike Doustdar—tapped to breathe new life into the Danish drugmaker last year after losing GLP-1 marketing ground to chief rival Eli Lilly—isn’t one to make changes for the sake of change. Nevertheless, the chief executive was acutely aware of the evolving perception of his company, both from within and without, in the build-up to its rebrand earlier this week.

The refresh spans many facets of Novo’s corporate identity, from the guiding principles of its business and purpose statement to the firm’s logo and name. Under the initiative, guided by the idea that “Lasting Health Starts Now,” the company’s everyday branding has been simplified to just “Novo,” while Novo Nordisk A/S remains its legal global moniker. Meanwhile, Novo’s mythologically-rich Apis bull logo—a hallmark of the company for decades—now faces right rather than left in a nod to the future.  

The decision to maintain and refresh the distinctive Apis bull logo signals that “it is good to be proud of your heritage, to still be a bull, but it’s also good—while you keep the integrity of who you are—to be open to changing directions from time to time,” Doustdar said in an interview with Fierce. 

But that desire to evolve did not come out of thin air. 

“Internally and externally, there is a recognition that Novo Nordisk needs to rethink and revise some parts of its strategy,” Doustdar said of how he’s framed the decision to colleagues. 

“Some parts are actually still very intact,” he said of Novo’s existing business. “Diabetes, obesity are very core to what we do, and we need to strengthen and continue that leadership.” That said, “there is more to that than we thought,” the Novo CEO admitted. 

Related

‘It’s been a roller coaster’: Novo Nordisk’s CFO reflects on ‘pressure’ to drive growth

Although Novo served as a trailblazer in unlocking the GLP-1 market, primarily through the prolific popularity of its type 2 diabetes medicine Ozempic and its sister semaglutide drug for obesity, Wegovy, the company has faced persistent challenges—particularly in the U.S. market—from Lilly, which itself markets direct incretin rivals in Mounjaro and Zepbound. 

More recently, the companies have embarked on a new competitive frontier via the launch of oral GLP-1 options for obesity, where Novo has been able to make the most of the head-start launch of its Wegovy pill in 2026. 

Against this backdrop, consumer behaviors have shifted rapidly as well, as people take more control over their health, aided by a groundswell of telehealth and virtual pharmacy services in recent years. 

“We make changes not for the sake of change,” Doustdar said. “We make changes as a response to the environment we are in, and our environment has been radically changed over the last three, four years, I would say, and we felt strongly that we needed to make some radical changes to adjust ourselves to it.” 

“But I also tell my colleagues,” Doustdar added, “that If we can find a good way to embrace change as humans, it would be very good because one thing is for sure: change will be the only constant in our future.” 

In terms of where Novo needs to adapt, Doustdar pointed to the company’s last purpose statement: We are here to drive change to defeat serious chronic diseases.

“Increasingly, the people we serve tell you that we cannot see ourselves in that statement,” he explained. 

He noted that many of Novo’s customers don’t consider themselves patients or people with a chronic disease, pointing specifically to those utilizing the company’s medicines for weight loss. 

“That disconnect makes you go back and think: How can I realign myself again to those I’m serving,” he added. 

“But when I think about ‘Lasting Health Starts Now,’ Doustdar said, “it also fits incredibly well to where we come from as a company and our diabetes heritage.”

“Diabetes is a progressive and chronic disease,” he explained. “We encourage and ask people to go on our medications, not least insulin, in order to avoid health complications in the future. In a very interesting way, we’ve been telling them for 100 years: Lasting health starts now.” 

On the other side of the coin, “instead of getting into a judgment call of what to call our customers or those we serve—patients or consumers—let’s talk about health,” Doustdar said. “Because at the end of it, for all of us, that’s most important.” 

Meanwhile, the new tagline “also opens up the room for us to explore more,” he added, pointing to “where the future will take us scientifically.” In particular, Doustdar suggested that this broader focus on lasting health would prevent Novo from having to rework its mission statement in the future should it wade into other fields of disease. 

 

Walking the walk

 

Beyond the company’s refreshed mantra, subtle changes to Novo’s corporate culture are expected to advance the company’s mission moving forward. 

“Strategy turns into execution by the right behaviors of those who are driving it,” Doustdar said, “and it would be borderline incomplete when you change the strategy and do not change the culture.” 

The four principles that will serve as Novo’s lodestar going forward—which it has dubbed “The Novo Way”—are customer obsession, competitiveness, clarity and, lastly, care and integrity. 

To the first point, Doustdar suggested that Novo must consider the patient in “everything that we do, from the onset of research to the delivery of the product to them.” 

As for the competitiveness piece, “it is really about not judging ourselves by what good looks like compared to yesterday,” Doustdar said, “but how fast others in the same field are running, and how can we be competitive vis-à-vis them?”

Clarity, meanwhile, primarily boils down to clear-eyed leadership, per the CEO, who warned that amid pressure to move quickly, “the fastest of all employees slows down and stands still when the leader is not very clear which direction they should be running towards.” 

“And last but not least,” Doustdar said, “having been here for 34 years, the care, the integrity of this company being second to none is so dear not just to me, but to all of our employees and to all of our customers, frankly speaking.” 

To that point, the CEO stressed that “it is possible to be competitive; it is possible to be assertive; it is possible to be fast, but still with care, still with integrity.”

In reflecting on Novo’s history and his time at the company, Doustdar opined that he was just 21 years old when he started with the drugmaker, noting that, at the time, “the company was very nervous because we had serious quality mishaps and problems with the FDA, and we were very close to possibly being closed out.” 

“The only ones that really believed in the company were us, the internal employees of the company,” he said. But rather than accept defeat, the Novo team at the time set out to “show the rest that our best days are ahead of us.”

Ultimately, that grit and determination helped Novo build what Doustdar described as “a quality system second to none, which we still today are incredibly proud of.” 

Looking back, Doustdar said that even when others see a mishap or hiccup and assume that Novo’s better days are behind them, “us as employees, we feel very different.” 

So far, internal reception to the changes has been positive, too, Doustdar noted. 

“I think they are quite happy to see the bull still alive,” Doustdar said of Novo’s workforce, “and when we tell them about the directional change, there is an ‘aha’ moment.” Meanwhile, the “simplicity and the pointiness” of Novo’s new quartet of guiding principles is going over well, too, he said. 

Related

‘I’m a lot more optimistic today’: Mike Doustdar tells Fierce about pivotal first year as Novo Nordisk CEO

Returning to Novo’s logo, Doustdar admitted that, “If anything, I joke around saying that if an Egyptian Apis bull of 3,000-year-old heritage can keep itself as a bull still, but go to the right, so can we also as humans.”

As for whether removing the bull from the logo was ever in question, Doustdar did not hesitate to explain, “absolutely not.”

data.title: Precision Medicine Has a Commercialization Problem
data.description:
By: Chris Paquette
Founder and CEO, DeepIntent

In 2023, BioMarin launched Roctavian, a drug promising new hope for patients with severe hemophilia. Approved as a one-time gene therapy, Roctavian was designed to improve quality of life by reducing the day-to-day burden of managing the disease. However, by 2026, Roctavian had been pulled from the market after failing to drive the adoption that BioMarin forecasted. This failure happened not because of Roctavian’s safety or efficacy as a therapeutic, but because BioMarin couldn’t commercialize this breakthrough treatment well enough to sustain it as a product. 

This isn’t the first example of a drug being pulled due to commercial failure. And, as AI enables and accelerates the development of treatments targeted at more precise patient groups, it won’t be the last.

AI is changing the way we think about drug development. We are already seeing how new drugs can be discovered faster and more efficiently than ever. Companies like Generate:Biomedicines and Pathos AI are securing major investment to bring new drugs to market using AI. And, while all patients may benefit from this watershed moment in R&D, patients with rare diseases stand to benefit the most. 

Indeed, orphan designations (treatments for conditions affecting less than 200,000 people in the U.S.) now exceed half of all new drug approvals annually. In both 2023 and 2024 combined, more than half of CDER’s novel approvals were for rare diseases or carried orphan designation, up from 38% only a decade prior. Furthermore, according to IQVIA, over 44% of treatments being pursued in development by pharma companies (from discovery through phase I-III of clinical testing) are designed to treat rare diseases. 

But for all the innovation and progress in drug discovery, there remains a major obstacle to the success of any new treatment: the cost and the complexity of getting these drugs into the hands of the patients who need them most. 

In order to commercialize new treatments, pharma companies must navigate a maze of regulators, providers, insurance companies, and pharmacy benefit managers. These stakeholders all demand evidence, education and active engagement. This requires significant time and investment into the commercial infrastructure – the teams, data, and systems powering go-to-market efforts – that can amount to hundreds of millions of dollars or more.

As a result, drug commercialization has traditionally been optimized for “blockbusters” – medicines treating patient populations often so substantial that they generate enough revenue to fund substantial commercial infrastructure while also generating returns large enough to fund the next generation of R&D. 

But what happens as precision medicine introduces more “long tail” therapies that address only thousands of patients? 

With a growing share of therapies targeting increasingly narrow addressable patient populations, our industry is heading towards a new economic collision: drugs designed to treat 5,000 patients simply cannot support the costs of bespoke commercial infrastructure in the same way that drugs treating 5 million patients do. If we don’t solve this, we will inadvertently create an invisible gate on innovation, care and outcomes, silently affecting millions of patients across the country and world.

This misalignment suggests that modernizing the commercialization process may be one of the most important challenges facing life sciences today and over the next decade. If we want personalized medicine to deliver on its full potential, we must re-think and re-build the infrastructure that supports developing, launching and sustaining increasingly personalized therapies in market in a more efficient way.

The good news is that the same technology accelerating drug discovery today may also help us redesign the economics of commercialization.

For more than a decade, as the founder and CEO of the healthcare marketing company DeepIntent, I have watched pharma marketing teams and their partners as they have embraced a relatively new technology – programmatic digital advertising – to connect scaled health datasets with the means to act and drive commercial outcomes more efficiently. By unifying that same data with AI-driven decision-making as well as broader process automation, marketers are already using AI to drive down costs for new patient engagement and drive adoption of new treatments more efficiently.

The impact is not theoretical. On Pfizer’s Q4 2025 earnings call, executives noted that AI was helping drive increased productivity and higher marketing return on investment, with promotional activity becoming “more targeted.”

But, as powerful as this AI impact has been, marketing represents only a fraction of the work required to support successfully commercializing a drug. At a minimum, any solution attempting to redesign the commercialization process needs to bring together a dizzying array of stakeholders and functions that each play a unique and vital role in ensuring commercial success. This includes teams responsible for finding unmet patient needs, proving value through evidence, and coordinating programs to raise awareness and reduce market friction for patients and their providers. 

To be clear, what we don’t need is another disconnected AI-powered point solution. What we need is a shared intelligence layer that connects the people who drive the commercialization process with the data, the insights, the capabilities, and each other more efficiently and quickly. 

Said another way, we need a more intelligent and collaborative system – a system that can more quickly identify constraints on product adoption, make recommendations on what to do next, and then act when feasible — all while improving confidence. It should be precise in showing which patients and providers to prioritize for outreach, which evidence gap to close, which access barrier to address, and where exactly the next dollar and hour of human effort should go. It should be built on trusted data and able to present actionable insights while encouraging collaboration and accelerating decision making.  

By better integrating the data these functions rely on and supporting them within one commercial intelligence layer, knowledge flows more easily through the organization, data becomes more actionable, and critical decisions get made faster and in more coordinated ways. 

The hardest part to achieving this vision may not even be the technology – it may be up-ending the rigidity of the processes and behaviors that drive commercialization today. 

But this is one area where agentic AI can be so powerful. By giving all stakeholders access to a shared AI interface, connected to a common commercial intelligence layer, we will incent the removal of technological and organizational barriers to progress, massively reduce time-to-insight, and significantly improve speed and cost-efficiency.  

A new commercial intelligence layer powered by agentic AI will accelerate the flow of information, empower teams with more current data to make better, more informed and more confident decisions. These teams will drive better commercial and clinical outcomes by knowing a more precise mix of which commercial “levers” to pull – and how hard it is to pull them. These decisions will be increasingly implemented as permissioned and governed actions, underwritten by connected data and actionable insights. Faster and more accurate decisions means less wasted time and duplicated work. 

But perhaps the most important effect will be that, with these efficiencies, the financial hurdle to successfully commercialize precision medicine will be substantially lowered. The minimum viable market size for new drugs will decrease, and with it, an entirely new class of targeted therapeutics will be made commercially viable.  AI will not only help us discover drugs to meet the needs of patients but help us deliver them.

We are already witnessing AI’s transformative effects on the field of medicine. But it’s increasingly clear that precision medicine will require precision commercialization. AI’s effect on the commercialization process is only just beginning, but with its rich and well-structured data, pharma presents as one of the most fertile targets for AI innovation.  Its application can not only improve efficiency for drug developers, but it can significantly improve the quality of life for hundreds of millions of Americans.   

****

Chris Paquette is the founder and CEO of DeepIntent, a healthcare marketing company that develops AI-enabled products enabling more efficient pharmaceutical commercialization. The views expressed are his own.

data.title: AbbVie chips in for neurology advocacy through PGA Tour campaign
data.description:
AbbVie has partnered with the PGA Tour and the 2026 Presidents Cup, teeing up the “Birdies for Brain Health” initiative to funnel cash to six patient advocacy organizations.

The agreement makes AbbVie, which reported $3.2 billion in neuroscience sales in the second quarter, the official pharmaceutical sponsor of the PGA Tour, a professional golf organization. This month’s 2026 Presidents Cup, a PGA Tour competition between U.S. and international golfers, marks the start of the alliance. 

AbbVie is launching “Birdies for Brain Health” at this month’s event, which is being held close to its home in North Chicago, Illinois. The drugmaker will kick off the campaign with a donation to patient advocacy organizations. 

Next year, AbbVie will expand the campaign and make donations for every birdie at PGA Tour Signature Events and the FedExCup Playoffs. A player achieves a “birdie” by completing a hole in one shot under par.

Gary Woodland, one of the U.S. captain’s assistants for the 2026 Presidents Cup, is working with AbbVie on the campaign. Woodland, the 2019 U.S. Open champion, underwent surgery in 2023 to remove a benign brain lesion and revealed a diagnosis of post-traumatic stress disorder this year. AbbVie will work with Woodland to bring the campaign “to life through storytelling and engagement.”

“My experience has shown me how important awareness, support and a strong community can be when someone is facing a health challenge," Woodland said in a statement. “‘Birdies for Brain Health’ gives us a meaningful way to use golf's platform to support organizations advancing science and patient advocacy, while helping people with brain health conditions and their care partners know they are not alone.”

AbbVie will split the donations between the American Migraine Foundation, the National Headache Foundation, Mental Health America, the National Alliance on Mental Illness, The Michael J. Fox Foundation for Parkinson’s Research and the Parkinson’s Foundation.

The patient advocacy groups cover the conditions treated by AbbVie’s neuroscience portfolio. AbbVie’s best-selling neuroscience drug is Vraylar, which is approved in major depressive disorder and bipolar I disorder. The company also markets Botox, Qulipta and Ubrelvy in migraine and Vyalev in Parkinson’s disease. Chronic migraine is one of 12 FDA-approved medical conditions for Botox.

AbbVie’s neuroscience sales increased 20% in the second quarter, with all the abovementioned products achieving double-digit growth. The drugmaker expects to win FDA approval for tavapadon in the third quarter, fueling its belief that it can generate peak Parkinson’s sales of more than $5 billion.
